content: The Zika virus can have significant implications for infant growth and development, particularly in cases where complications arise. Primary caregivers and parents of infants affected by Zika virus-related complications may face additional social, educational, and financial challenges that could further impact the developmental outcomes of their children. The recommendations provided align with previous WHO guidelines on breastfeeding promotion, protection, and support in maternity and newborn care facilities, as well as counseling women to improve breastfeeding practices. The development of these guidelines followed a standardized process as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. This process included identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, evaluation, and updates. The WHO Guideline Steering Committee, composed of staff from various WHO departments and regional offices, managed the guideline development process. They drafted key questions in PICO format, identified systematic review teams and guideline methodologists, and organized the Guideline Development Group and external review groups. The committee also supervised evidence synthesis, organized meetings, finalized the guideline document, and managed dissemination and impact assessment. The Guideline Development Group included experts in infectious diseases, neonatology, infant feeding, and nutrition policies. Members were selected to ensure geographical representation and minimize conflicts of interest. Gender diversity was considered, though not explicitly consulted. Fifteen external experts and stakeholders were invited to participate, bringing expertise in research, guideline development methods, clinical policy, and infant health and nutrition programs. Two online meetings were convened. During the first meeting, the group discussed the scope of the guideline, key questions, and outcomes to guide evidence reviews and recommendations. In the second meeting, members reviewed and reached consensus on the strength and direction of the recommendations, considering the balance of benefits and harms, evidence certainty, stakeholder values, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, human rights, and equity. Systematic reviews were commissioned to inform the guideline, including evidence on Zika virus transmission through breast milk, modified feeding practices, and caregiver support for infants affected by Zika-related complications. Qualitative reviews explored the perspectives of pregnant women, mothers, family members, healthcare practitioners, and policymakers on infant feeding in the context of Zika virus risks and congenital Zika syndrome. The WHO Guideline Steering Committee used evidence profiles to summarize findings from systematic reviews. These profiles, along with GRADE tables and other relevant documents, were shared with the Guideline Development Group before the second meeting. Members provided comments electronically and during discussions, which informed the final recommendations. The group agreed on three types of recommendations: recommended, context-specific, and not recommended. Decisions were based on the importance of the effect to end-users rather than statistical significance. The group reached unanimous consensus on the recommendations. To manage conflicts of interest, all potential members completed WHO declaration forms and provided updated CVs. The WHO Steering Committee reviewed these declarations and assessed potential intellectual biases. Public disclosure of interests was required, and any concerns were addressed with the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. Members with declared interests participated fully after public disclosure. The decision-making process involved reviewing evidence summaries, preliminary judgments, and comments. Additional criteria from the GRADE evidence-to-decision framework, such as stakeholder values, resource implications, and equity, were applied. Evidence-to-decision tables synthesized these considerations, and final decisions were made using an online tool. All members reviewed and revised the draft recommendations, achieving unanimous consensus. Before the online meeting, the WHO Steering Committee prepared draft documents, including GRADE evidence profiles and evidence summaries, which were shared with participants for comments. These documents were discussed and revised during the meeting. Afterward, questions were refined, and members reached consensus. A preliminary version of the final document was sent for peer review to five independent experts not involved in the guideline development group. Their inputs were evaluated for inclusion, and modifications were limited to correcting factual errors and improving clarity. The guideline will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, health ministries, professional organizations, collaborating centers, and other United Nations agencies.
